name: The Bug Analyst
oneLiner: Rolls every bug under a feature into a computed status report — fix rate, time-to-fix, hotspots, per-assignee load — with zero manual tallying.
lead: Walks a feature (or an explicit story list) down to its child Bug work items, enriches each with a computed days-to-fix, aggregates the whole set in memory, and emits a shareable report set: JSON, Markdown, a multi-sheet Excel workbook, and optionally Word. Replaces the afternoon-in-spreadsheets with a single deterministic pass.
chore: Briefing a lead means opening the tracker and hand-tallying: open vs fixed, severity mix, which area has the most, who's carrying the load, mean time-to-fix — then pasting it into a doc. Hours of work, stale the next day, and arithmetic errors creep in by hand.
instead: An instant, reproducible report — totals by severity/state, fix rate, average days-to-fix, the hotspot story, per-assignee workload, plus generated insights and recommendations — as Markdown, Excel, JSON, and optionally Word. Every number is computed from live tracker data, so it's right every run.
whyItMatters: Go/no-go calls ride on these numbers. Getting them fast and correct is the difference between a confident ship and a nasty surprise — and computed beats hand-tallied every time.

howItWorks.step: Given a feature or story list, walks each story's hierarchy and collects its child Bug work items.
howItWorks.explain: The hierarchy walk that feeds everything downstream. For each `storyId` it fetches the work item **with its relations** (a normal fetch omits them), captions it (falling back to `Story #<id>` when the title is blank), then pulls only the **outbound** `Hierarchy-Forward` links via `extractRelationIds` — that direction means *children*, so a bug's own parent link is never mistaken for a child. Empty child sets `continue` early to skip a pointless batch call, and `getWorkItemsBatch` requests a **fixed field projection** (not the whole work item) in one round-trip per story, keeping ADO calls down. The `child.fields?.['System.WorkItemType'] === 'Bug'` guard drops sibling Tasks/Test-Cases so only Bugs are enriched.

howItWorks.step: Normalizes each raw work item into a typed `EnrichedBug` with a computed days-to-fix.
howItWorks.explain: The normalization boundary — every downstream aggregate reads `EnrichedBug`, never raw ADO JSON. `daysToFix` is derived only when **both** `resolvedDate` and `createdDate` are present; the ms delta is converted to days (`1000*60*60*24`), `Math.round(x*10)/10` snaps it to **0.1-day** resolution, and `Math.max(0, …)` clamps negatives — a real defense, since ADO's `ResolvedDate` can predate `CreatedDate` after a bug is edited or re-imported, which would otherwise poison the mean. Unresolved bugs deliberately keep `daysToFix = null` (not `0`) so the aggregator can **exclude** them rather than average in a fake zero. The `raw.id ?? f['System.Id'] ?? 0` chain and every `|| ''` / `|| 'Unspecified'` fallback guarantee a fully-populated typed record even when ADO omits a field, and `extractDisplayName` collapses the `AssignedTo` identity object down to a plain name string.

howItWorks.step: Single-pass aggregation: totals by severity/state, fix rate, mean days-to-fix, per-assignee workload.
howItWorks.explain: The single-pass aggregator — one `for` loop over `bugs` buckets everyone into `assigneeMap`, with `bug.assignedTo || 'Unassigned'` so null-assignee bugs still count somewhere instead of vanishing. Note that `FIXED_STATES` (`Resolved`/`Closed`) and `OPEN_STATES` (`New`/`Active`) are **not** exhaustive — a bug in a custom state like `Removed` increments neither counter, which is why `open + fixed` can be less than `total` and the numbers stay honest rather than force-fitting every state. `fixRate` divides `fixedBugs` by the **full** `bugs.length` (with a `> 0` guard against divide-by-zero on an empty feature), while `avgDaysToFix` first filters to `daysToFix !== null` so unresolved bugs never drag the mean toward zero — an all-open feature yields `null`, not `0`, again snapped to 0.1-day precision. Every metric comes from this one in-memory sweep — no second ADO query.

howItWorks.step: Emits threshold-triggered insight strings — hotspot story, sub-50% fix rate, an assignee with ≥ 3 open bugs.
howItWorks.explain: Deterministic, threshold-fired commentary — no LLM, so the same stats always produce the same lines. It relies on `perStory` already being **sorted descending by bug count**, so `perStory[0]` is by definition the hotspot; the `hotspot.bugCount > 0` guard suppresses the line on a clean feature. The fix-rate warning is gated on `< 0.5` **and** `totalBugs >= 3` together — the minimum-sample guard stops a single unfixed bug (a 0% rate over one item) from reading as a systemic problem. For load, `perAssignee.find(a => a.openBugs > 0)` takes the **first** entry with open work (the list is pre-sorted, so that's the most-loaded person), and the `>= 3` cutoff means only a genuine pile-up surfaces. Each line is pushed conditionally, so `insights` can legitimately come back empty — silence means nothing crossed a threshold.

howItWorks.step: Derives actionable recommendations from the same stats — prioritize Critical/High, triage backlog, flag untested stories.
howItWorks.explain: The action-oriented sibling of `generateInsights` — same deterministic threshold style, but each line is a *thing to do*. `critHigh` sums the `1 - Critical` and `2 - High` buckets off `bySeverity` with `|| 0` fallbacks so a missing severity key reads as zero instead of `NaN`, and any non-zero total recommends prioritizing before sprint end. The zero-bug filter inverts the usual hotspot logic — a story with `bugCount === 0` is treated as **suspicious**, likely *untested* rather than genuinely clean, so it nudges you to confirm test execution actually started; the offending IDs are joined into one readable line. Finally `openBugs >= 5` recommends a formal triage session — a higher bar than the per-assignee `>= 3` insight because this is about the whole feature's backlog. Like insights, `recs` can return empty when nothing qualifies.

howItWorks.step: Serializes the report to a multi-sheet Excel workbook (plus JSON/Markdown/Word alongside).
howItWorks.explain: The serialization step — `xlsx` is `require`d lazily inside the function, not imported at module top, so a `--dry-run` that never writes files pays nothing for the dependency. It builds the workbook as an **array-of-arrays** (`aoa_to_sheet`): each inner array is one row, an empty `[]` renders a blank spacer row, and the `['Metric','Value']` row acts as a header. Two presentation choices matter — `s.fixRate` (a 0–1 float) is multiplied by 100 and suffixed `%` for a human-readable cell, and `s.avgDaysToFix ?? 'N/A'` uses `??` (not `||`) so a legitimate **zero** average survives while only `null`/`undefined` become `'N/A'`. Each sheet is appended by name via `book_append_sheet`, and `writeFile` flushes the whole `.xlsx` to `outputPath` in one call.

examples.caption: Pre-standup sanity check
examples.input: A handful of story IDs with `--dry-run`.
examples.output: On-screen tally only — `Total bugs: 14, mostly Medium, 4 open` — no files written. Glance and go.

underHood.heading: Hierarchy walk to child bugs
underHood.whenRuns: First, from a feature or story list.
underHood.input: A feature ID or story IDs.
underHood.output: Every child Bug work item, batch-fetched from ADO.

underHood.heading: Field normalization + days-to-fix
underHood.output: A typed `EnrichedBug` with computed `daysToFix`, ready to aggregate.

underHood.heading: In-memory aggregation
underHood.output: Totals by severity/state, fix rate, avg days-to-fix, per-assignee load — one pass, no extra queries.

underHood.heading: Threshold insights + recommendations
underHood.output: Rule-fired lines flagging hotspots, sub-50% fix rate, and overloaded assignees, plus recommended actions.

underHood.heading: Multi-format serialization
underHood.output: JSON, Markdown, an `xlsx` workbook, and — with `--word` — a `.docx` with embedded bug screenshots.

prerequisites: Node ≥ 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
An Azure DevOps org/project and a **PAT** with work-item read scope.
A feature ID (top-down discovery) or a list of story IDs to roll up from.
No LLM key — metrics, insights, and recommendations are all rule-computed, not model-generated.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the runtime.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is TypeScript on Node. One-time per machine.
steps.firstRun: First time only, on a new machine.

steps.label: Clone and install dependencies.
steps.why: `npm install` pulls the ADO client and the `xlsx`/report writers into `node_modules`.
steps.firstRun: Full install, a minute or two.
steps.rerun: No-op once installed, unless the dependency list changed.

steps.label: Export the ADO target (environment variables).
steps.cmd:
export ADO_ORGANIZATION=my-org
export ADO_PROJECT="My Project"
export ADO_PAT=your-access-token
steps.why: Read at startup to resolve the org/project and authenticate the read queries.

steps.label: Dry-run to tally bug counts on-screen.
steps.cmd:
npm run bug:intel -- --feature-id 4001 --dry-run
# or a targeted list of stories:
npm run bug:intel -- --parent-ids "4010,4013,4060" --dry-run
steps.why: `--dry-run` walks the hierarchy and aggregates on-screen without writing files — a fast check before the full serialization.
steps.firstRun: Reads every story and bug under the feature fresh.

steps.label: Generate the full report set.
steps.cmd:
npm run bug:intel -- --feature-id 4001
# add a Word document too:
npm run bug:intel:word -- --feature-id 4001
steps.why: Drops `--dry-run` and serializes the report files to disk.
steps.rerun: No caching — every run re-queries live ADO data, so it always reflects current counts and picks up bugs filed since last run.

steps.label: Open the report.
steps.why: The `.md` is the at-a-glance summary; the `.xlsx` holds the sortable bug list and severity-by-state pivot for a deeper cut.

inputs.name: --feature-id <id>
inputs.desc: Feature ID — auto-discovers child stories and their bugs, top-down.

inputs.name: --parent-ids <ids>
inputs.desc: Comma-separated story IDs to target instead of (or alongside) a feature.

inputs.name: --feature-name <name>
inputs.desc: Optional report-header label, if you don't want it auto-fetched.

inputs.name: --dry-run
inputs.desc: On-screen tally only — no files written.

outputs.name: BugIntel_<timestamp>.json
outputs.desc: Full structured report — totals, fix rate, per-story and per-assignee breakdowns, insights, recommendations.

outputs.name: BugIntel_<timestamp>.md
outputs.desc: The same report rendered for at-a-glance reading.

outputs.name: BugIntel_<timestamp>.xlsx
outputs.desc: Multi-sheet workbook: Summary, All Bugs, Per-Story, severity-by-state pivot.

runbook.rerun: Nothing to warm — every run queries ADO fresh, so a second run reflects whatever changed since (newly filed, newly fixed). Schedule it to keep the report current with zero manual tallying.
runbook.integrate: Point it at a fixed `--feature-id` in a nightly/weekly CI or cron job; pipe the `.xlsx`/`.json` into a dashboard, or drop the `.md` straight into a status channel — it's authored to be posted as-is.

video.caption: A 2-3 minute screen recording: point it at a feature ID and watch the computed status report serialize.
script: Open a terminal beside the team's work board so viewers see both.
Say: 'This agent turns a pile of bug tickets into the manager's status report. Watch.'
Run `node -v` to confirm Node is installed; one line on what Node is.
Run `npm install` (or note it's already done); explain it's grabbing the tracker client and report writers.
Show the `export ADO_ORGANIZATION / ADO_PROJECT / ADO_PAT` lines; say this is the only project-specific config.
Run `npm run bug:intel -- --feature-id 4001 --dry-run`; narrate the on-screen tally as it appears.
Run it again without --dry-run and with --word; explain it's now writing the full report set to disk.
Open the produced `.md`; read out the fix rate, the hotspot story, and one insight line.
Open the `.xlsx`; show the per-story and severity-by-state sheets.
Close: 'Same numbers, every time, in the time it takes to read this sentence.'
